#### IRAS — GST

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**GST input tax claim eligibility and supporting documentation** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS allows an input tax claim only when all applicable conditions are met: the claimant is GST-registered; the goods or services are supplied to or imported by it and are used for its business; local purchases have valid tax invoices and imports have the required import permits and supporting documents; the input tax is attributable to qualifying taxable or specified out-of-scope supplies; the claim is not disallowed under Regulations 26 or 27; and the claimant has taken reasonable steps to conclude that the goods or services are not part of a Missing Trader Fraud arrangement, on a conclusion a reasonable person would make. A conclusion about a particular purchase also requires the GST-registration status, what was acquired and its business use, the related supplies, supporting documents, any applicable blocked-input-tax exception, and the Missing Trader Fraud assessment. outcomes.response:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

#### IRAS — GST

**Status:** Evidence verified

**GST return filing deadline, nil-return duty, and extension procedure** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** A GST return and any tax due are generally due one month after the accounting period ends. A nil return is still required when there was no business activity. For GIRO, deduction is on the 15th of the month after the payment due date, shifted to the next working day if it falls on a weekend or public holiday. Extensions are generally not granted; IRAS considers only acceptable reasons, requires a request with supporting documents at least five working days before the due date, and if the request is not approved before the due date, late filing penalties apply and the outstanding GST F5 must be filed immediately. [GST Filing Due Dates and Requests for Extension | Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) (offline fixture title)](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/filing-gst/gst-filing-due-dates-and-requests-for-extension)

**Source:** GST Filing Due Dates and Requests for Extension | Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) (offline fixture title) (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST return filing deadline, nil-return duty, and extension procedure): You must file a “Nil” return even if you had no business activity during the accounting period.

Filing and payment due dates

Your GST return and payment are due 1 month after the end of your accounting period. If you pay via GIRO, IRAS will deduct payment on the 15th day of the month after the payment due date. If the deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

Without GIRO

GST Accounting Period  | File and pay by

Jan - Mar  | 30 Apr

Apr - Jun  | 31 Jul

Jul - Sept  | 31 Oct

Oct - Dec  | 31 Jan

With GIRO

GST Accounting Period  | File by | GIRO deduction Date

Jan - Mar  | 30 Apr  | 15 May

Apr - Jun  | 31 Jul  | 15 Aug

Jul - Sept  | 31 Oct  | 15 Nov

Oct - Dec  | 31 Jan  | 15 Feb

Note: To confirm that your GST will be paid via GIRO, check the acknowledgement page after you file your GST F5 return.

Filing due date for special accounting periods

If you have special GST accounting periods, your return is due 1 month after the end of that accounting period.

Example: If your period runs from 5 Apr 2026 to 5 Jul 2026, your return is due on 5 Aug 2026.

Penalties for late filing and payment

Penalties will apply if you are late in filing your GST return and making payment.

Requesting an extension to file

As one month after the end of your accounting period is a reasonable deadline, extensions are generally not granted. You are expected to maintain proper transaction tracking systems and ensure you have adequate resources to file on time.

Reasons that will not be accepted

No extension will be granted for the following reasons:

• Staff on maternity leave

• Director or key accounts personnel are overseas

• Staff have resigned without proper handover

• Closing of accounts at year-end

• New accounts personnel do not know how to handle GST matters

• No computer

• Not enough manpower to handle GST matters

Acceptable reasons for extension

We may grant an extension only if your request arises from one of the acceptable reasons below:

Acceptable reasons for extension | Documents required  | Maximum extension granted

Newly GST-registered businesses filing their first GST return  | Nil  | 1 month

Breakdown of IT system  | e.g. IT servicing report  | 2 weeks

Purchase of a new accounting software or IT system | Tax invoice | 2 weeks

Key accounting personnel on long medical leave (more than 1 week)  | Medical/ hospitalisation certificates  | 2 weeks

Restructuring of company  | e.g. Notice of restructuring, media release  | 2 weeks

Software issues or errors encountered when submitting GST returns via seamless filing software through API | Nil | 2 weeks

How to submit your request

Submit your extension request form at least 5 working days before the filing due date, together with all required supporting documents.

Note: Requests submitted late or after the filing due date will not be processed. If your request is not approved before the due date, late filing penalties will apply. You will also be required to file the outstanding GST F5 immediately.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally requires ECI filing within three months after FYE. The general waiver requires both annual revenue of S$5 million or less for that financial year and nil ECI for the YA, with ECI measured before partial or start-up exemption. Revenue is the company’s main source of income; for an investment holding company it is investment income. A nil ECI or book loss alone does not qualify a company whose relevant revenue exceeds S$5 million; likewise, revenue below the threshold does not qualify when ECI is positive. IRAS gives separate entity categories that need not file and says companies self-assess the waiver. To assess a particular YA, confirm FYE, principal/investment revenue, pre-exemption ECI and any specifically excluded category. [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Source:** IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions): ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions): Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions): Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions): Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions): Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions): If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions): If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.
- Official source: [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Whether no accounting profit establishes the ECI filing waiver** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally requires ECI filing within three months after FYE. The general waiver requires both annual revenue of S$5 million or less for that financial year and nil ECI for the YA, with ECI measured before partial or start-up exemption. Revenue is the company’s main source of income; for an investment holding company it is investment income. A nil ECI or book loss alone does not qualify a company whose relevant revenue exceeds S$5 million; likewise, revenue below the threshold does not qualify when ECI is positive. IRAS gives separate entity categories that need not file and says companies self-assess the waiver. To assess a particular YA, confirm FYE, principal/investment revenue, pre-exemption ECI and any specifically excluded category. [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Source:** IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Whether no accounting profit establishes the ECI filing waiver): ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Whether no accounting profit establishes the ECI filing waiver): Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Whether no accounting profit establishes the ECI filing waiver): Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Whether no accounting profit establishes the ECI filing waiver): Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Whether no accounting profit establishes the ECI filing waiver): Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Whether no accounting profit establishes the ECI filing waiver): If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Whether no accounting profit establishes the ECI filing waiver): If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.
- Official source: [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed, and application to the case remains unresolved

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**Withholding-tax applicability to specified non-resident payments** (party in scope: Company)
- **Application unresolved:** For Withholding-tax applicability to specified non-resident payments, case-specific treatment or calculation has not been verified. The relevant facts and statutory conditions still need to be established.

**Source:** IRAS | Payments that are subject to withholding tax (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding-tax applicability to specified non-resident payments): With effect from 1 Nov 2022, this administrative concession will be withdrawn. Withholding tax will be applicable to any cost reimbursement payment liable to be made on or after 1 Nov 2022 to a non-resident related party, even if the payment is made under a cost-pooling arrangement.

CPF Ordinary Wage ceiling | CPF annual salary ceiling

From 1 Sep to 31 Dec 2023 | $6,300 (+$300)

From 1 Jan to 31 Dec 2025 | $7,400 (+$600)

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)

Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.

Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.

Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status

CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.

Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.

Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)

Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.

Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. Authority: CPF Board, Government of Singapore
Page title: How much CPF contributions to pay
Canonical official URL: https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/how-much-cpf-contributions-to-pay
Capture date (Singapore): 2026-10-27
Capture method: verbatim visible text returned by a read-only browser extraction of the official HTML page. This is not a raw HTML response; exact excerpt text is retained below.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

**Facts required to calculate an employee’s CPF contributions** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board selects the contribution table from citizenship or SPR year, age group and wage band. Total wages combine Ordinary Wages (OW) and Additional Wages (AW), which have separate ceilings. For wages above S$50 and up to S$500 in a month, the employee share is nil but the employer share remains due. Round the combined total contribution to the nearest dollar (50 cents rounds up); drop cents from the employee share and set the employer share to total less employee. To determine the actual amount, supply the payroll month, date of birth, status/PR conversion date, rate election, CPF-classified OW/AW, year-to-date contributions and expected annual OW where an AW ceiling applies. Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**Facts required to calculate an employee’s CPF contributions** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board selects the contribution table from citizenship or SPR year, age group and wage band. Total wages combine Ordinary Wages (OW) and Additional Wages (AW), which have separate ceilings. For wages above S$50 and up to S$500 in a month, the employee share is nil but the employer share remains due. Round the combined total contribution to the nearest dollar (50 cents rounds up); drop cents from the employee share and set the employer share to total less employee. Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF Additional Wage ceiling formula and Ordinary Wage offset** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board sets the AW ceiling per employer, per year at S$102,000 less that employee’s Ordinary Wages subject to CPF for the year. The 2026 examples use an OW ceiling of S$8,000 per month and say the year in which an AW is due and payable controls the ceiling. At each AW payment, estimate OW for the year and account for AW already subject to CPF. In the last month of employment or December, whichever is earlier, recalculate using actual OW subject to CPF through that period; pay any CPF shortfall with the last-month or December contributions, and apply for a refund if excess CPF contributions result. To compute the current payment’s CPF-subject AW, the employer must provide actual year-to-date OW/AW and either the expected full-year OW or confirm this is final settlement. [Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/069IW00000KUuZCYA1)

**Source:** Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF Additional Wage ceiling formula and Ordinary Wage offset): Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling
The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.
- Official source: [Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/069IW00000KUuZCYA1)

The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.
- Official source: [Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/069IW00000KUuZCYA1)

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Employment Act eligibility start for paid annual leave): Annual leave eligibility and entitlement
If you are covered by the Employment Act and have worked for at least 3 months, you are entitled to annual leave.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Employment Act eligibility start for paid annual leave): Eligibility
You are entitled to paid annual leave if you have worked for your employer for at least 3 months.
You can only apply for annual leave after working for 3 months.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Employment Act eligibility start for paid annual leave): Entitlement
Your annual leave entitlement depends on how many years of service you have with your employer. Your year of service begins from the day you start work with your employer.
Year of service | Days of leave
1st | 7
2nd | 8
3rd | 9
4th | 10
5th | 11
6th | 12
7th | 13
8th and thereafter | 14
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Employment Act eligibility start for paid annual leave): How pro-rated annual leave is calculated
Annual leave is pro-rated using this formula: (Number of completed months of service ÷ 12 months) × Number of days of annual leave entitlement.
If the fraction of a day is less than one-half, round it down.
If it is half or more, round it up to one day.
The period from 14 to 31 July is disregarded as it is not a completed month.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Employment Act eligibility start for paid annual leave): If you are taking unpaid leave
You should exclude periods of approved unpaid leave when calculating your annual leave entitlement.
If you have taken unpaid leave, your employer can pro-rate your leave entitlement based on how many complete months you have worked.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Employment Act eligibility start for paid annual leave): If you are serving notice
If you have resigned, your notice period is included when calculating your pro-rated annual leave.

How pro-rated annual leave is calculated

**Private-company small-company audit exemption criteria** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** Small-company audit exemption requires the entity to be a private company in the financial year and to meet at least two of the three quantitative criteria for each of the immediate past two consecutive financial years: revenue no more than S$10 million, assets no more than S$10 million, or no more than 50 full-time employees at FYE. A company that is less than two years old is assessed against criteria in its current year. A group also has to meet the separate consolidated small-group criteria. Two of three criteria must hold for both immediately preceding consecutive financial years for an established company; “this year and last year” does not always establish that period. The Singapore company and the entire group (including foreign entities) must each satisfy their respective test where the company is part of a group. A qualifying company remains qualified until it ceases to be private or no longer meets at least two criteria over the immediate past two consecutive financial years. The current-year test applies to a newly incorporated private company less than two years old. A separate dormant-company audit exemption may apply; do not confuse audit exemption with relief from preparing financial statements or filing an annual return. A case-specific conclusion requires: Private-company status during the financial year. Revenue, total assets and full-time employee count for the immediate past two consecutive financial years. If part of a group, the consolidated figures and entire-group scope. Whether the company is newly incorporated or another audit exception is being considered. A company-specific conclusion needs two financial years’ facts and, for a group, consolidated facts. Audit exemption does not exempt a company from keeping proper records, preparing financial statements, annual-return filing or tax filing. [Audit exemptions: Small company concept | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/preparing-financial-statements/audit-exemptions/)

To qualify for audit exemption as a small company, you need to meet both of these criteria:

•

• Your company is a private company in the financial year; and

•

•

• Your company meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:

•

◦

◦ Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards

◦

•

◦

◦ Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards

◦

•

◦

◦ 50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year

◦

•

If your company is newly incorporated (less than two years old)

You qualify for audit exemption if you meet the criteria in the current financial year.

Example:

•

• First financial year: Check if you are a private company and meet two out of three quantitative criteria that year.

•

•

• Second financial year: If you did not qualify in the first year, check again using the same requirements for the second year.

•

If your company is part of a group

You need to meet both of these conditions to qualify for audit exemption:

•

• Your Singapore company or subsidiary qualifies as a small company; and

•

•

• Your entire group (including foreign entities) meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:

•

◦

◦ Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards

◦

•

◦

◦ Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards

◦

•

◦

◦ 50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year

◦

•

Note: The audit exemption applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 July 2015.

Maintaining your exemption status

Once your company qualifies as a small company, you remain qualified in subsequent financial years unless:

•

• You cease to be a private company at any time during a financial year; or

•

•

• You do not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years

•

Once your group qualifies as a small group, it remains qualified for subsequent financial years. This applies until it does not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

Yes, you can qualify for audit exemption even if you have corporate shareholders.

Unlike the previous criteria, you do not need to be an exempt private company to qualify for audit exemption.

No, it does not change your financial statement filing requirements.

Yes, audit exemption is for private companies.

Section 205B of the Companies Act exempts a dormant company from audit requirements. A dormant company is not limited to a private company.

Section 205C read with the Thirteenth Schedule of the Companies Act exempts a small company from audit requirements. This exemption is only applicable to private companies.

In deciding whether a company should be treated as a small company or a small group for the purpose of being exempted from audit requirements, the company would need to refer to section 205C read with the Thirteenth Schedule of the Companies Act. In particular, para 12(a) of the Thirteenth Schedule of the Companies Act states that “the question whether an entity is part of a group is to be decided in accordance with the Accounting Standards”.

If the company is owned by another company (i.e. parent company), it will need to assess whether it belongs to a small group, regardless of whether it prepares and/or file consolidated financial statements.

The assessment will be based on the past two years financials.

On whether a company is a small company or a small group for the purpose of being exempted from audit requirements, the company would have to refer to section 205C read with the Thirteenth Schedule of the Companies Act. In particular paras. 7, 8 and 9 of the Thirteenth Schedule set out the situations in which the criteria for audit exemption should be applied to the first financial year of consolidation or the two financial years preceding the financial year of consolidation.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**Number of size criteria required for the small-company audit exemption** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** Small-company audit exemption requires the entity to be a private company in the financial year and to meet at least two of the three quantitative criteria for each of the immediate past two consecutive financial years: revenue no more than S$10 million, assets no more than S$10 million, or no more than 50 full-time employees at FYE. A company that is less than two years old is assessed against criteria in its current year. A group also has to meet the separate consolidated small-group criteria. Two of three criteria must hold for both immediately preceding consecutive financial years for an established company; “this year and last year” does not always establish that period. The Singapore company and the entire group (including foreign entities) must each satisfy their respective test where the company is part of a group. A qualifying company remains qualified until it ceases to be private or no longer meets at least two criteria over the immediate past two consecutive financial years. The current-year test applies to a newly incorporated private company less than two years old. A separate dormant-company audit exemption may apply; do not confuse audit exemption with relief from preparing financial statements or filing an annual return. A case-specific conclusion requires: Private-company status during the financial year. Revenue, total assets and full-time employee count for the immediate past two consecutive financial years. If part of a group, the consolidated figures and entire-group scope. Whether the company is newly incorporated or another audit exception is being considered. A company-specific conclusion needs two financial years’ facts and, for a group, consolidated facts. Audit exemption does not exempt a company from keeping proper records, preparing financial statements, annual-return filing or tax filing. [Audit exemptions: Small company concept | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/preparing-financial-statements/audit-exemptions/)

- **ACRA rule explanation:** Small-company audit exemption requires the entity to be a private company in the financial year and to meet at least two of the three quantitative criteria for each of the immediate past two consecutive financial years: revenue no more than S$10 million, assets no more than S$10 million, or no more than 50 full-time employees at FYE. A company that is less than two years old is assessed against criteria in its current year. A group also has to meet the separate consolidated small-group criteria. Two of three criteria must hold for both immediately preceding consecutive financial years for an established company; “this year and last year” does not always establish that period. The Singapore company and the entire group (including foreign entities) must each satisfy their respective test where the company is part of a group. A qualifying company remains qualified until it ceases to be private or no longer meets at least two criteria over the immediate past two consecutive financial years. The current-year test applies to a newly incorporated private company less than two years old. A separate dormant-company audit exemption may apply; do not confuse audit exemption with relief from preparing financial statements or filing an annual return. A case-specific conclusion requires: Private-company status during the financial year. Revenue, total assets and full-time employee count for the immediate past two consecutive financial years. If part of a group, the consolidated figures and entire-group scope. Whether the company is newly incorporated or another audit exception is being considered. A company-specific conclusion needs two financial years’ facts and, for a group, consolidated facts. Audit exemption does not exempt a company from keeping proper records, preparing financial statements, annual-return filing or tax filing. #### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**Private-company small-company audit exemption criteria** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** Small-company audit exemption requires the entity to be a private company in the financial year and to meet at least two of the three quantitative criteria for each of the immediate past two consecutive financial years: revenue no more than S$10 million, assets no more than S$10 million, or no more than 50 full-time employees at FYE. A company that is less than two years old is assessed against criteria in its current year. A group also has to meet the separate consolidated small-group criteria. Two of three criteria must hold for both immediately preceding consecutive financial years for an established company; “this year and last year” does not always establish that period. The Singapore company and the entire group (including foreign entities) must each satisfy their respective test where the company is part of a group. A qualifying company remains qualified until it ceases to be private or no longer meets at least two criteria over the immediate past two consecutive financial years. The current-year test applies to a newly incorporated private company less than two years old. A separate dormant-company audit exemption may apply; do not confuse audit exemption with relief from preparing financial statements or filing an annual return. A case-specific conclusion requires: Private-company status during the financial year. Revenue, total assets and full-time employee count for the immediate past two consecutive financial years. If part of a group, the consolidated figures and entire-group scope. Whether the company is newly incorporated or another audit exception is being considered. outcomes.response:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** Additional case facts or checks are required; see the issue-level limitations.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**Simplified VCFM licensing path and admission eligibility** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** At a high level, MAS describes a VCFM as an LFMC that operates under a simplified VCFM regime. A company that solely manages venture capital funds may apply to use this route. MAS says VCFMs follow simplified admission criteria; the cited page points to Appendix 4 but does not give a full side-by-side comparison or its detailed criteria. The route requires an application and is not automatic eligibility. MAS also considers the business model and risks, risk and compliance controls, track record and expertise, fitness and propriety, minimum financial requirements, and dedicated secure office arrangements; check Appendix 4 before deciding whether a particular manager qualifies. [Fund Management Licensing | Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) (offline fixture title)](https://www.mas.gov.sg/regulation/capital-markets/apply-for-licensing-or-registration-of-capital-market-entities/fund-management-licensing)
- **Application unresolved:** For Simplified VCFM licensing path and admission eligibility, case-specific treatment or calculation has not been verified. The relevant facts and statutory conditions still need to be established.

**Source:** Fund Management Licensing | Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) (offline fixture title) (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Simplified VCFM licensing path and admission eligibility): If your company solely manages venture capital funds, it may apply to be an LFMC that operates under the simplified venture capital fund manager (VCFM) regime.

Individuals performing key functions in a fund management company, such as portfolio construction and allocation, research and advisory, business development and marketing or client servicing are required to be representatives.

You can find out more about fund management activity and the differences between an LFMC and VCFM here.

When we assess your company to be an LFMC or VCFM, MAS considers factors such as:

• Credibility and substantiveness of the business model and plan, and the associated risks;

• Effectiveness of risk management and compliance controls;

• Fund management track record and expertise of an LFMC applicant's management, parent company and major shareholders;

• Fitness and propriety of the applicant, its shareholders and directors; and

• Ability to meet the relevant minimum financial requirements prescribed under the SFA.

In addition, your company needs to operate from a dedicated and secure office space that is accessible only by your company’s directors and staff.

For more information on the admission criteria and applicable requirements, please refer to the Guidelines on Licensing and Conduct of Business for Fund Management Companies.

VCFMs are subject to a simplified set of admission criteria – please refer to Appendix 4 of the aforementioned guidelines.
- Official source: [Fund Management Licensing | Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) (offline fixture title)](https://www.mas.gov.sg/regulation/capital-markets/apply-for-licensing-or-registration-of-capital-market-entities/fund-management-licensing)

• Fitness and propriety of the applicant, its shareholders and directors; and

• Ability to meet the relevant minimum financial requirements prescribed under the SFA.

In addition, your company needs to operate from a dedicated and secure office space that is accessible only by your company’s directors and staff.

Filing due date for special accounting periods

If you have special GST accounting periods, your return is due 1 month after the end of that accounting period.

Example: If your period runs from 5 Apr 2026 to 5 Jul 2026, your return is due on 5 Aug 2026.

Penalties for late filing and payment

Penalties will apply if you are late in filing your GST return and making payment.

Requesting an extension to file

As one month after the end of your accounting period is a reasonable deadline, extensions are generally not granted. You are expected to maintain proper transaction tracking systems and ensure you have adequate resources to file on time.

Reasons that will not be accepted

No extension will be granted for the following reasons:

• Staff on maternity leave

• Director or key accounts personnel are overseas

• Staff have resigned without proper handover

• Closing of accounts at year-end

• New accounts personnel do not know how to handle GST matters

• No computer

• Not enough manpower to handle GST matters

Acceptable reasons for extension

We may grant an extension only if your request arises from one of the acceptable reasons below:

Acceptable reasons for extension | Documents required  | Maximum extension granted

Newly GST-registered businesses filing their first GST return  | Nil  | 1 month

Breakdown of IT system  | e.g. IT servicing report  | 2 weeks

Purchase of a new accounting software or IT system | Tax invoice | 2 weeks

Key accounting personnel on long medical leave (more than 1 week)  | Medical/ hospitalisation certificates  | 2 weeks

Restructuring of company  | e.g. Notice of restructuring, media release  | 2 weeks

Software issues or errors encountered when submitting GST returns via seamless filing software through API | Nil | 2 weeks

How to submit your request

Submit your extension request form at least 5 working days before the filing due date, together with all required supporting documents.

Note: Requests submitted late or after the filing due date will not be processed. If your request is not approved before the due date, late filing penalties will apply. You will also be required to file the outstanding GST F5 immediately.

- **IRAS rule explanation:** A GST return and any tax due are generally due one month after the accounting period ends. A nil return is still required when there was no business activity. For GIRO, deduction is on the 15th of the month after the payment due date, shifted to the next working day if it falls on a weekend or public holiday. Filing and payment due dates

Your GST return and payment are due 1 month after the end of your accounting period. If you pay via GIRO, IRAS will deduct payment on the 15th day of the month after the payment due date. If the deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

Without GIRO

Jan - Mar  | 30 Apr

Apr - Jun  | 31 Jul

Jul - Sept  | 31 Oct

Oct - Dec  | 31 Jan

With GIRO

GST Accounting Period  | File by | GIRO deduction Date

Jan - Mar  | 30 Apr  | 15 May

Apr - Jun  | 31 Jul  | 15 Aug

Jul - Sept  | 31 Oct  | 15 Nov

Oct - Dec  | 31 Jan  | 15 Feb

Note: To confirm that your GST will be paid via GIRO, check the acknowledgement page after you file your GST F5 return.

Filing due date for special accounting periods

If you have special GST accounting periods, your return is due 1 month after the end of that accounting period.

Example: If your period runs from 5 Apr 2026 to 5 Jul 2026, your return is due on 5 Aug 2026.

Penalties for late filing and payment

Penalties will apply if you are late in filing your GST return and making payment.

Requesting an extension to file

As one month after the end of your accounting period is a reasonable deadline, extensions are generally not granted. You are expected to maintain proper transaction tracking systems and ensure you have adequate resources to file on time.

Reasons that will not be accepted

No extension will be granted for the following reasons:

• Staff on maternity leave

• Director or key accounts personnel are overseas

• Staff have resigned without proper handover

• Closing of accounts at year-end

• New accounts personnel do not know how to handle GST matters

• No computer

• Not enough manpower to handle GST matters

Acceptable reasons for extension

We may grant an extension only if your request arises from one of the acceptable reasons below:

Acceptable reasons for extension | Documents required  | Maximum extension granted

Newly GST-registered businesses filing their first GST return  | Nil  | 1 month

Breakdown of IT system  | e.g. IT servicing report  | 2 weeks

Purchase of a new accounting software or IT system | Tax invoice | 2 weeks

Key accounting personnel on long medical leave (more than 1 week)  | Medical/ hospitalisation certificates  | 2 weeks

Restructuring of company  | e.g. Notice of restructuring, media release  | 2 weeks

Software issues or errors encountered when submitting GST returns via seamless filing software through API | Nil | 2 weeks

How to submit your request

Submit your extension request form at least 5 working days before the filing due date, together with all required supporting documents.

Note: Requests submitted late or after the filing due date will not be processed. If your request is not approved before the due date, late filing penalties will apply. You will also be required to file the outstanding GST F5 immediately.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Estimated Chargeable Income filing deadline and general waiver conditions** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally requires ECI filing within three months after FYE. What is the Ordinary Wage (OW) ceiling?
The Ordinary Wage (OW) ceiling sets the maximum amount of OW that attracts CPF contributions in a calendar month for all employees. It was gradually raised and has reached $8,000 in 2026. The increase took place in four steps, as shown in the table below, to allow employers and employees to adjust to the changes.
Table: Changes in CPF salary ceilings
CPF Ordinary Wage ceiling | CPF annual salary ceiling
From 1 Jan 2016 to 31 Aug 2023 | $6,000 | $102,000 (no change)
From 1 Sep to 31 Dec 2023 | $6,300 (+$300)
From 1 Jan to 31 Dec 2024 | $6,800 (+$500)
From 1 Jan to 31 Dec 2025 | $7,400 (+$600)
From 1 Jan 2026 | $8,000 (+$600)

The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a

The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year

$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)

according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.

**Employee and employer CPF contribution rate factors** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF contribution rates depend on citizenship or permanent-resident status (including the applicable PR year), age group, and total wages or wage band. Use the rate table effective for the contribution period being assessed. This is a general explanation and does not determine an employee’s rate or calculate contributions. - **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Employee and employer CPF contribution rate factors): CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
- Official source: [CPF | How much CPF contributions to pay](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/how-much-cpf-contributions-to-pay)

CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**Facts required to calculate an employee’s CPF contributions** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board selects the contribution table from citizenship or SPR year, age group and wage band. Total wages combine Ordinary Wages (OW) and Additional Wages (AW), which have separate ceilings. For wages above S$50 and up to S$500 in a month, the employee share is nil but the employer share remains due. Round the combined total contribution to the nearest dollar (50 cents rounds up); drop cents from the employee share and set the employer share to total less employee. To determine the actual amount, supply the payroll month, date of birth, status/PR conversion date, rate election, CPF-classified OW/AW, year-to-date contributions and expected annual OW where an AW ceiling applies. [CPF | How much CPF contributions to pay](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/how-much-cpf-contributions-to-pay)
- **Application unresolved:** For Facts required to calculate an employee’s CPF contributions, case-specific treatment or calculation has not been verified. The relevant facts and statutory conditions still need to be established.
